title: One Hundred One Unuseless Japanese Inventions
author: Kenji Kawakami
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: If the use of tools is what first set mankind on the road to civilization, what does the new "art and philosophy" of Chindogu -- Japanese for "odd or distorted tool" -- reveal about our prospects at the dawn of the 21st century? We "have the luxury to build that which we can't really use," explains Kenji Kawakami, a former cartoon scriptwriter, bicycle museum designer and home shopping magazine editor who now devotes himself to subverting the Japanese obsession with gadgets and technology. His latest book, 101 UNUSELESS JAPANESE INVENTIONS: The Art of Chindogu (Norton, paper, $10.95), may also subvert the American notion that he and his countrymen are conformist robots, lacking the genes for whimsy and anarchy. A Chindogu, as Mr. Kawakami puts it (with the help of his translator, Dan Papia), is an almost useless invention, something that looks as if it's going to make your life easier -- and only succeeds in making it more ridiculous. Like the hay fever hat, a roll of paper tissues that sits snugly on the sufferer's head, fresh sheet dangling handily just above eye level. Or the golfer's practice umbrella, equipped with a club head at the tip,  perfect for chip shots on a subway platform. Admittedly, some Chindogu may speak to distinctly Japanese social needs: consider, for example, the sweetheart's training arm, an extra appendage that attaches to a coat or jacket, recommended  for "the early stages of courting" to avoid "the worry of sweaty palms, inappropriate pressure or when to disengage." Then again, what married woman of  any nationality hasn't yearned for the back scratcher's T-shirt stamped with a handy "itch-locater grid," the perfect garment for a demanding mate? Or, better  still, the dust and shake, a combination duster and martini shaker that rewards  vigorous cleaning, providing a truly fine incentive for tackling room after room after room. Mr. Kawakami may have strayed from his absurdist mandate on that one. It seems to me the height of civilized invention.   ALIDA BECKER

pull_quote: The life and work of the Italian photographer Tina Modotti (1896-1942) have become fodder for such a variety of causes that Sarah M. Lowe's vow to write Modotti's "cultural biography" and "dislodge her from the center of her legend"  may cause cynics' eyebrows to arch in suspicion. Yet, as the author's intelligent introductory essay to the 150 elegant duotone photographs reproduced in TINA MODOTTI: Photographs (Philadelphia Museum of Art/Abrams, $45) soon makes clear, Ms. Lowe means what she says. She has done extensive research about the political, social and cultural contexts of Modotti's many whereabouts. Tina  Modotti was an uneducated working-class girl in turn-of-the-century Italy and a  sophisticated actress, muse and femme fatale in Hollywood before spending the years from 1923 to 1930 in Mexico, where she became an increasingly political photographer; later, among other activities, she was a relief worker in the Spanish Civil War. Ms. Lowe, an art historian and curator, puts the facts of Modotti's life in illuminating perspective, tracing the artist's esthetic development, her ties to the Modernist movement and her awareness of the conflict between making art and making politics. If "Experiment in Related Form" (1924) -- a double exposure of five glasses of differing sizes whose rims seem to float, intersect and shine all at once -- means freedom from the austere esthetic of Edward Weston, Modotti's lover and teacher of photography, the sea of sombreros in "Workers Parade" (1926) marks Modotti's first expression of her  disappointment with the unfulfilled promises of the Mexican revolution and her commitment to a new social order. From portraits of Aztec mothers with their infants to "Mella's Typewriter" (a close-up of a Communist lover's instrument of intellectual and political activity), Modotti's tight cropping and still-life esthetic excelled at melding Mexican culture and Modernist photography.   CHRISTINE SCHWARTZ HARTLEY

pull_quote: If it is evil to care too much for things that have neither mind nor heart,  then I am evil," Harriet Doerr writes in the first of the 15 pieces of memoir and short fiction in THE TIGER IN THE GRASS: Stories and Other Inventions (Viking, $19.95). This is far too hyperbolic a statement. Ms. Doerr does have a  sure and elegant hand when it comes to describing flora and fauna and the houses in California and Mexico where she has lived. But with her keen attention to detail in matters of character and emotion, she demonstrates a compassionate spirit that is anything but evil. Using an episodic structure similar to those in her novels, "Stones From Ibarra" and "Consider This, Senora," this new book allows Ms. Doerr to contemplate certain events from the nearly nine decades of her life, even as she returns us to the locales made familiar in her fiction. Writing with admirable simplicity, she recalls spending sublime childhood summers at the beach, knitting a muffler for an American soldier in France (who  sent her a much-cherished thank-you note) and going off to Smith College in 1927. There are also memories of being widowed at 65 after 42 years of marriage  and then going back to college, and of helplessly standing by as her son began to succumb to cancer. Several of the short stories, set in Ibarra, reacquaint readers with Sara and Richard Everton, who were introduced in Ms. Doerr's first  book. Others explore different parts of rural Mexico. Like the matilija poppies  of Ms. Doerr's youth, "whose crushed tissue-paper petals unfolded every June into white flowers as big as a child's face," these previously uncollected short works are strikingly pure and radiant. SALMAN RUSHDIE'S new novel, his first since the infamous fatwa issued by the  Iranian Government in 1989 as punishment for putatively blasphemous passages in  his satire "The Satanic Verses," comes heavily attended by certain inevitable questions. How is Mr. Rushdie holding up after six years in hiding? What kind of story is the world's most famous living author, in this extraordinary situation, going to tell us and, of course, himself? Is this another book that will give offense, and to whom? Will this book comment, directly or otherwise, on the dogma-driven expansion of censorship and persecution affecting writers in so many parts of the world? It's only when we've worked through this vanguard of questions that we're free to ask what we can take from this novel, as opposed to all the novels it competes with -- serious novels whose ambitions are to show us what we urgently need to know or feel in this threatening moment, when alarms and grim forewarnings crowd in on us, making so many of our innocent pastimes feel difficult to justify, fiction reading itself not excepted.

pull_quote: In the mid-1930's, a young French ethnographer named Claude Levi-Strauss ventured by rail, truck, canoe and horseback into the Brazilian interior to document the cultural habits of tribal groups whose numbers and customs were still somewhat protected by their relative isolation. Equipped with a Leica and  "an oval-shaped miniature 8-mm. camera whose name I have forgotten," the anthropologist, feeling ambivalent about the use of photography in such a setting, nonetheless created a rare visual record of archery contests, funeral rites, face painting and other traditional customs, some of which have long since been abandoned. The photographs of the Nambikwara, the Bororo and the Caduveo form the centerpiece of Mr. Levi-Strauss's SAUDADES DO BRASIL: A Photographic Memoir (University of Washington, $39.95), skillfully translated from the French by Sylvia Modelski. There are also images of Sao Paulo in the 1930's when it was a frontier city of "singular beauty" and not yet one of the industrial capitals in the world, and of pristine Brazilian landscapes that now, in large or small part, bear the scars of mining and logging as well as other ravages of modernization. The reader might be surprised at the remarkable, if rueful, candor with which the renowned anthropologist introduces the volume: "The photographs leave me with the impression of a void, a lack of something the lens is inherently unable to capture." Although Mr. Levi-Strauss, a chief architect of structural anthropology, declares that he is not a photographer, "not even an amateur," the images here are skillful and compelling. But it is not the quality of the photographs he is apologizing for; it is history. And his apology is not directed at us so much as at the ghosts of his tribal subjects, "the last escapees from the cataclysm" of European colonialism and its aftermath.   SUZANNE MacNEILLE

AT 71, Josef Skvorecky remains an ironist, a disposition granted him by nature and by the successive totalitarian regimes under which he lived until he  emigrated from Czechoslovakia to Canada in 1968. In his novels, Mr. Skvorecky writes with the skeptical authority of an ironic witness to tragic events. He approaches matters of principle offhandedly, as if to remind the reader how indelicately principles are adduced in an absolutist state. "Faith?" asks one of his characters in the aftermath of the Prague Spring. "Where, except maybe in a  madhouse, is there any faith left to be lost?" Yet Mr. Skvorecky's novels abound in faith, though it's guarded by the self-exposing irony of a writer. So it is remarkable to come upon "The Bride of Texas" (it was published in Czech in 1992). Mr. Skvorecky has set this work among a group of Bohemian-born soldiers during the final weeks of the American Civil War, when Gen. William Tecumseh Sherman was marching northward through South Carolina in a landscape set alight  by withdrawing rebel forces and by stray elements of his own advance troops called "bummers." At the end, Sherman would turn away from a climactic battle at Bentonville, N.C., because he knew the war was almost over and because, as he says, war "is not an exercise in mass execution."

THE Colorado Plateau was the last blank spot on the map in the contiguous United States. Not a single plateau but a labyrinth of plateaus, canyons, peaks  and desert basins occupying adjacent parts of Utah, Arizona, New Mexico and Colorado, the region remained unexplored until the mid-19th century. Since then, it has inspired some of our best thinking and writing about wild nature and humanity's relationship with it. Arid climate and rugged terrain provided seminal opportunities for the developing sciences of geology and archeology. Anasazi cliff dwellings remained remarkably well preserved 700 years after their abandonment, and sedimentary strata provided a record of evolution since the Paleozoic Era. Writers like Wallace Stegner, Ann Zwinger and Edward Abbey have made the plateau a major literary region.

pull_quote: Alberto Manguel's foreword to A BLUE TALE AND OTHER STORIES (University of Chicago, $14.95), a posthumous volume by Marguerite Yourcenar, explains that the three "curiosities" collected here, written between 1927 and 1930, when the author was in her mid-20's, shed light on her artistic development and life. While fruitful critical and biographical connections can be drawn between the stories and Yourcenar's formidable oeuvre -- particularly "Memoirs of Hadrian," "Alexis" and "Oriental Tales" -- the stories also stand on their own.  As translated by Mr. Manguel, the prose of the young Yourcenar is accomplished and her vision arrestingly mature. In the first story, "A Blue Tale," European merchants set out to plunder a cave full of sapphires on a Middle Eastern island only to meet failure, death and destitution. The spare recitation and repeated use of the color blue prove to be haunting features in this fable of greed, in which a woman catches sapphires in her hair for the merchants; after she is cruelly kidnapped, her tears turn to aquamarines. In "The First Evening," initially written by Yourcenar's father and revised by her at his request, a jaded, self-absorbed man travels with his young wife to their honeymoon in Switzerland. His fear of life's banality, which engulfs him as he approaches his conjugal bed, is momentarily abated by a telegram announcing the death of his former mistress, who still preoccupies him. The last story, "An Evil Spell," further reveals Yourcenar's imaginative powers as she describes a witch hunt, set somewhere near the Mediterranean in southern France. Here a woman named Algenare is deemed to have cast an evil spell on a woman she envies. Pointing up the human need for scapegoats, Yourcenar illustrates how naming and becoming are one, as the villagers brand Algenare a witch and Algenare herself finds in the night sky "in large trembling strokes, the giant letters of the witches' alphabet." For its insight into human frailty and vice, for its language forged  with precision and nuance, this slim trio of tales is richly rewarding.   GARDNER MCFALL

title: Poland, 1946: The Photographs And Letters Of John Vachon
author: John Vachon
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: In 1946, a young American photographer named John Vachon was sent to Poland by the recently formed United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration to document that agency's aid efforts in a country suffering from the catastrophic ravages of World War II. Vachon (1914-75), who had been part of a distinguished photographic team working for the Farm Security Administration in  the 1930's, did not much relish doing official publicity shots, and most of the pictures he took in Poland were put away in archives without being published; but, as they are collected in POLAND, 1946: The Photographs and Letters of John Vachon (Smithsonian Institution, $39.95), they bring back, with  a startling poignancy, a time that for most of us is a forgotten historical zone. In Poland, perhaps more than in most of Europe, the war didn't really finish with its official end; and in his trips across the country, Vachon everywhere found the evidence of a continuing battle for survival, of massive social rearrangement and of still-seething political conflicts. Cities in rubble, children with rickets, villages burned to cinders by underground units fighting the newest Soviet domination, inhabitants of formerly German cities being deported, repatriates from Eastern territories being transported in filthy boxcars: this could be a terribly depressing record -- and yet, oddly, it isn't. In his letters to his wife, Vachon, despite his political naivete, wrote with great understanding not only about the hardships he witnessed, but also about the courage and dignity of the people he encountered -- and his images convey this fundamental sympathy. In the many faces of strangely grown-up children, in  the eyes of repatriates looking up with stubborn gravity, in the haunting melancholy of lone figures among ruins, in a family of peasants against a moody  rural landscape or a row of women salvaging bricks from a crumbled building, Vachon repeatedly caught both the pain of what had happened and the sense of fierce life reasserting itself. These impressionistic and somberly beautiful photographs constitute a deeply affecting portrait of a place and a people struggling to emerge from a terrible war into an uneasy peace.   Eva Hoffman

pull_quote: Hollywood is sure to ruin SHOOT! (St. Martin's, $22.95), an absorbing, panoramic novel set in the waning Wild West days of British Columbia. It's that  good: intricately plotted, meticulously researched and shaded with nuance. In "Shoot!" the Canadian poet and novelist George Bowering tells the story of four  young men whose Indian mothers and white fathers earn them the dismissive status of half-breeds. Caught between two cultures that neither understand nor accept them, the boys tumble self-destructively from petty thievery to murder. With page after page of thundering hoofbeats, shoot-outs and blood-red sunsets, Shoot! does the western genre proud. But what truly distinguishes this novel is  Mr. Bowering's unflinching examination of bigotry and intolerance, which seems as relevant to today's world as to that of the 1870's. Steady doses of wit and adventure help his brusque prose recover from occasional didactic detours, and a spiraling narrative structure gives the old-fashioned setting some post-modern flair. A brilliant colorist whose work is often seen as falling somewhere  between representation and abstraction, Mr. Hodgkin "does not allow illustration to interfere with the making of a painting," Mr. Auping writes. "Memory and metaphor are his preferred terrain." Mr. Auping finds that Mr. Hodgkin's paintings of the last two decades have forged the unlikely pairing of Intimism and Expressionism from wildly diverse influences like Henri Matisse, douard Vuillard, Barnett Newman, Jackson Pollock, Jasper Johns and Willem de Kooning. (Both Vuillard and opera, so to speak.)" Along with 80 color illustrations are an erudite and informative epistolary exchange between Mr. Hodgkin and John Elderfield, the chief curator at large at the Museum of Modern Art, and the first catalogue raisonn of Mr. Hodgkin's oil paintings, compiled by Marla Price, the director of the Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth. author: Eve Arnold
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: It was time," says the octogenarian photographer Eve Arnold, "to make an archive . . . to make order out of the chaotic files that have been my life." For a photojournalist who has published eight previous books and accumulated more than 40 years' worth of slides, negatives and prints, that is a tall order. EVE ARNOLD: In Retrospect (Knopf, $50) is a chronological memoir of Ms. Arnold's professional life along with the photographs by which she wants to be remembered. From images of Malcolm X, Marilyn Monroe and Margaret Thatcher to those of anonymous veiled Afghan women and of toddlers in a Chinese nursery, the shots she has chosen show not only the high points but also the broad sweep of her undertakings. Throughout her career, she has worked for Magnum, the photographers' cooperative founded by Robert Capa, Henri Cartier-Bresson, George Rodger and David Seymour, usually on assignment for publications like Life and London's Sunday Times. Her style, despite her confession to "dithering and nerves," is authoritative and humanist -- energized, as she says, by the unfamiliar. Being there is paramount to a photojournalist's success, and Ms. Arnold gives a lively account of the obstacles she surmounted -- rough terrain,  illness, intractable bureaucrats. Although few of the book's images hold the transcendent power of her color picture of an old Chinese woman whose beautifully lined face emerges from the textured black of her clothes and the surrounding shadow, all attest to her enterprise and tenacity, along with her ability to establish rapport with her subjects. As Ms. Arnold looks back, she seems justifiably pleased with her accomplishments and wonders about her next project. Now that she has achieved order, she might try another kind of memoir,  a distillation of her memories that brings more of the woman herself into focus.   Rosemary Ranck

title: American Exceptionalism: A Double-Edged Sword
author: James P Pinkerton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote:
To assert that America is exceptional, as analysts have been doing since Tocqueville, is to dwell on paradox. In "American Exceptionalism: A Double-Edged Sword," Seymour Martin Lipset motes that while the United States is the most litigious society in the world -- spending four to eight times as much on lawsuits as Germany, England, Italy, France, the Netherlands or Japan -- it is simultaneously one of the most lawless, vexed by crime rates triple those of other industialized nations. Hence America's double-edged sword: on one side of  the blade, "a high sense of personal responsibility, independent initiative and  voluntarism"; on the other side, "self-serving behavior, atomism and a disregard for communal good." 

      Central to Mr. Lipset's American exceptionalism is the idea of a definable American Creed, "a set of dogmas about the nature of a good society," deriving mostly from the Revolution. These include liberty, egalitarianism (defined as equality of opportunity, not result), individualism, populism and laissez-faire. To buttress his argument, he uses copious survey data to demonstrate how different America is from other advanced countries. For example, in 1992 just 38 percent of Americans agreed that government should reduce the difference in income between rich and poor, compared with 65 percent of Britons, 66 percent of West Germans and 80 percent of Italians.

Milne (Free Press, $24) briskly examines the authors of five classics of British children's literature and offers shrewd assessments of those profoundly eccentric men and their great works. Each of the writers, Ms. Wullschlger says, "needed a child as muse to trigger the adult imagination into creating an extraordinary fantasy. Once locked into this magical world, however, each drew on his own peculiarly strong affinity with childhood." The key there is "peculiarly," because, as she  discreetly puts it, "all shared a reluctance to engage in conventional behavior  and relationships." The creation of those fantasy lands, she argues, was made possible by, and in turn reflected, "the confidence and prosperity of Britain between 1860 and 1914." It was a confidence that "lasted until the First World War, when to die ceased to be the awfully big adventure that Peter Pan had expected." Ms. Wullschlger, a literary critic and feature writer at The Financial Times in London, thinks that A. A. Milne's work from the 1920's belongs with the others because it was "a throwback" and "nostalgically desperate" for what had been lost. While she is insightful and clear about all five writers, she is particularly good on Edward Lear. She does not hesitate to  address Lear's homosexuality, but she insightfully notes that his relationships  with children "had none of the anguished, knowing intensity of Carroll's or Barrie's." Lear, she says, "made child-friends and then let them go, as easily and carelessly as a child on holiday would." "The Owl and the Pussycat," that most beloved nonsense lyric about "two odd, sexless, cozy lovers," was written shortly after Lear was talked out of making a proposal of marriage to a much younger woman, she observes, and it is a poem of "hopeful escape." pull_quote: A HISTORY OF FASCISM, 1914-1945 By Stanley G. Payne. Illustrated. 613 pp. Madison: The University of Wisconsin Press. $39.95.    IS fascism a thing of the past? The question has both a theoretical and a practical interest. On the theoretical side we are curious whether fascist movements and regimes are so linked to the conditions of Europe between the world wars that nothing having their peculiar combination of features can be found in other historical contexts -- such as our own. Practically, we are anxious about the future of liberal democracy. We wonder if the increase in economic insecurity that affects almost all of us -- but particularly the middle classes, for whom it remains in some ways a novel experience -- may not provoke  a revival of movements of the kind that swept away fragile democracies in the 1930's. Looking at the world around us, it seems that powerful fascist movements do belong to the interwar period and pose no major danger to us now. Except perhaps for Russia, where Vladimir Zhirinovsky's bizarrely misnamed Liberal Democratic Party has evoked comparisons with Hitler's National Socialists in Weimar Germany, no democratic state faces anything that could reasonably be described as a fascist threat. Most democracies contain small groups that are estranged from democratic institutions, some of them -- like those who inspired  the Oklahoma bombing or those who daubed European synagogues with anti-Semitic slogans -- willing to resort to terrorist violence. Yet none of these groups are in a position to mount a challenge to a democratic state. Can we then safely write off fascism as largely banished from the world?

title: Saving Graces: Images Of Women In European Cemeteries
author: David Robinson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: They wilt, they swoon, they languish. What's more, they're naked, or mostly naked, or at least some of them are. In his afterword to SAVING GRACES: Images of Women in European Cemeteries (Norton, cloth, $25; paper, $14.95), a collection of more than 100 of his black-and-white photographs of marble, stone  and bronze maidens in various degrees of distress, David Robinson notes that these statues, most of them made in the mid- to late 19th century, serve as surrogate mourners and embody the Romantic notion of the link between love and death. And who can say him nay, especially after seeing the uninhibited figure from Genoa's Staglieno cemetery, passed out backward in apparent ecstasy, barely draped and with a posy of roses tucked in her armpit? Ecstatic, too, is the fully draped maiden in Pre Lachaise in Paris, about to be raised to heaven by a  well-muscled angel who is hovering above her with a display of more than brotherly (or perhaps sisterly -- it's hard to tell) interest. But the high-relief carving of a kneeling nude in the Staglieno, roses held strategically in her lap, is as unemotional and non-erotic as could be. And how  about the figure of the draped young girl in Paris's Passy cemetery who looks not only demure but totally unconcerned about such matters as love and death? No roses, but her attributes include a Greco-Etruscan helmet and a carved replica of a Bernard Palissy ceramic platter, which leads one to wonder whose monument this is, and why these particular artifacts are to the point. But why quibble? The photographs are beautiful, and beautifully reproduced.   Sarah Ferrell

pull_quote: Julie Taymor is one of the most remarkable theater artists of the last two decades, though she unfortunately remains known to only a relatively small group of cognoscenti. Like the works she creates, Ms. Taymor is not easily classifiable; she is a director, a designer, a mask and puppet maker, a choreographer, film maker and fabulist. She creates worlds of visual splendor and an almost childlike fantasy that, like good fairy tales, reveal grotesquerie and even horror just barely beneath the surface. Her work as a designer and director reflects her literal and artistic journeys through Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bali, Japan and Paris and her apprenticeships with Joseph Chaikin, Herbert Blau and the Bread and Puppet Theater. This background has resulted in productions of Shakespeare, opera and original works in which the visual, the narrative and the symbolic are inseparable. Ms. Taymor integrates techniques and esthetics from a wide variety of theatrical cultures. But unlike  some contemporary directors who seem to plunder other cultures for inspiration only to come up with mere superficial borrowings, she creates a unique yet somehow familiar vocabulary that, as Eileen Blumenthal, a professor of theater arts at Rutgers University, says in her highly readable JULIE TAYMOR, PLAYING WITH FIRE: Theater, Opera, Film (Abrams, $49.50), is a "new theatrical organism." Ms. Taymor, who collaborated on the book with Ms. Blumenthal, describes each of the 15 productions she has designed or directed since her work in Bali in the mid-1970's. This book will be of interest to anyone who wonders where the magic, spirit and theatricality of the theater have gone in recent times, or to anyone who values the visual and creative imagination. author: Ernest Alfred Vizetelly
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Originally published in 1873 and until now not easily available in English translation, mile Zola's novel THE BELLY OF PARIS (Sun and Moon, paper, $14.95)  recounts the sad story of Florent, a young schoolteacher sent to prison after being falsely accused of resisting Louis Napoleon's coup d'tat in 1851. At the novel's opening, seven years have passed; Florent has escaped and returned to Paris half dead of starvation only to find himself lost in the sprawling, Lucullan new markets of Les Halles, overwhelmed by "an avalanche of food." These markets provide the book's true focus, as Zola chronicles the vigorous, greedy intrigues of butchers, fishwives, poultry sellers and butter dealers, all of whom feel first irritated, then threatened by the sight of this morose, idealistic, skinny young man. To Florent, the markets "appeared symbolical of some glutted, digesting beast, of Paris, wallowing in its fat and silently upholding the Empire" that has treated him so cruelly. Clearly that's also how they appeared to Zola, who, in Ernest Alfred Vizetelly's translation, minutely describes this "colossal belly" -- from the damp, odorous fish stalls to the mountains of fleshy produce in the vegetable and fruit pavilions. As Florent becomes increasingly repelled by Louis Napoleon's mercantile Paris and begins to plot an ill-fated insurrection, these descriptions turn monstrous. Never before  has cheese seemed so sinister: "A Livarot was swarming with life; and in a fragile box behind the scales a Grom flavored with aniseed diffused such a pestilential smell that all around it the very flies had fallen lifeless on the  gray-veined slab of ruddy marble." The novel's appeal lies, of course, in Zola's descriptive brilliance, his ability to paint this brutal, teeming world of food  with the confidence of a Dutch master. But the political conflict, personified by scrawny Florent and the overfed shopkeepers, is artfully rendered as well. This is not a book for dieters -- or those with delicate stomachs.   Suzanne Berne

title: In The Alleys: Kids In The Shadow Of The Capitol
author: Laura Goldstein
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: In the years following the Civil War, emancipated slaves poured into the nation's capital, often ending up in cramped and hidden alley neighborhoods. Overcrowding and lack of sanitation attracted reformers, and by the turn of the  century a movement to eradicate these pestilential areas was under way. Reform legislation, urban planning schemes, two wars and documentary photographers like Lewis Hine came and went before the neighborhoods were finally razed in a redevelopment effort in the 1950's. In 1943, a social worker named Godfrey Frankel (1912-95) took his camera and rode a bicycle into one of these alleys, ready to expose the capital's squalid underside. To his surprise, what he discovered during repeated afternoon forays was something richer and more complex -- a community and its children, which are portrayed in IN THE ALLEYS: Kids in the Shadow of the Capitol (Smithsonian, cloth, $55; paper, $24.95), with text by Laura Goldstein, a freelance Washington journalist, and a foreword by the photographer Gordon Parks. Mr. Parks also visited the alleys in the early 1940's, and describes them as dirty, disgruntled and gloomy, but Frankel's images portray a more benign environment. The sun raking across the uneven brick passageways and peeling wooden steps where troops of small children gather suggest stability and warmth. When Frankel's subjects face his camera, their expressions range from grave to gleeful, their integrity never in doubt. Ragged  clothes become symbols of pluck and resourcefulness rather than despair. Ms. Goldstein provides an affectionate biography of Frankel and a history of the Washington alleys. By including comments by middle-aged survivors of alley childhood, she adds depth to this record of an eradicated past.   Rosemary Ranck

title: Rumpole And The Angel Of Death
author: John John Clifford Mortimer Mortimer
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: First-rate comic writing is often more difficult to produce than the serious  stuff, and real pros are few and far between. One of these is John Mortimer, an  Englishman best known in this country for his mystery stories starring the comic and gallant barrister Horace Rumpole. Mr. Mortimer knows his territory, and his  comments on the vagaries of the English legal system and the small value it places on common sense and moral standards are as sharp as ever in RUMPOLE AND THE ANGEL OF DEATH (Viking, $22.95), the 10th volume of stories in the series. In Rumpole, Mr. Mortimer has created a wonderfully durable and attractive character, henpecked as a husband but masterful with a jury, an honest man whose only cause is "preventing the conviction of the innocent." Rumpole's true home is the courtroom, but we are also made privy to life in the gloomy flat in Froxbury Mansions where he exists in pitiful thralldom to his wife, Hilda, otherwise known as She Who Must Be Obeyed. This moniker notwithstanding, the forbidding Hilda has occasional moments of decency, and Rumpole fans will be amused to find one story narrated by Hilda herself, in which she reveals surprisingly romantic yearnings as she contemplates an affair with a smarmy colleague of her husband's. In his happy ability to play a seemingly infinite number of diverting variations on the same theme, in the fluidity and panache of his prose, his combination of high intelligence and low foolery, John Mortimer is worthy of comparison to P. G. Wodehouse. "Rumpole and the Angel of Death," like all of the preceding Rumpole volumes, makes for ideally civilized light reading.   Brooke Allen

title: Robert Doisneau: A Photographer'S Life
author: Peter Hamilton
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Near the end of ROBERT DOISNEAU: A Photographer's Life (Abbeville, $75), Peter Hamilton explains that his book was "supposed to be the 'definitive' monograph" about the French photographer, born in 1912, who spent his life documenting the sometimes lonely beauty, enduring romance and comic contrasts he found in Paris and its suburbs from the 1920's to the 80's. A sociologist, Mr. Hamilton was clearly able to understand that Doisneau's art was deeply rooted, reflecting both his pride of place and his humanism. A typical photograph from the 30's shows carefree boys watching a merry-go-round. A shot of a coal ration  card against a snow-covered Paris Opera illustrates the hardships of the occupation. A photograph of unkempt children in an empty, cobblestoned Paris square speaks of France's dreary 50's; and new suburban concrete overpasses and  modern apartment buildings show up in Doisneau's late pictures. Doisneau's death in 1994, before the book's completion, obviously came as a personal loss for the author. "Robert Doisneau: A Photographer's Life" is less exhaustive than it appears, for all its nearly 400 dense, oversized pages, with almost as many striking duotone and color reproductions, and the appendixes and interviews. For one thing, many of the book's pages could have been better used to show photographs and to provide details about projects only mentioned in passing, rather than to describe Doisneau's very static life (he inhabited the same suburban apartment from 1937 on and almost never traveled abroad). Most important, Mr. Hamilton eschews any real discussion of Doisneau's frequent use of models, actors and mises-en-scne in order to re-create scenes of daily life.  His world-famous 1950 photograph "Baiser de l'H/tel de Ville," for instance, was far from being documentary; it was staged. Without an exploration of the practice of presenting as candid something that isn't, and of the ethical and photo-historical questions it raises, a monograph about Doisneau can't be definitive.   Christine Schwartz Hartley

author: William K Marimow
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Since 1977, Camilo Jose Vergara, a native Chilean, has been training his camera on some of the poorest neighborhoods in several of this country's poorest cities. His photographs, with accompanying text, record an intriguing but often  depressing landscape in THE NEW AMERICAN GHETTO (Rutgers University, $49.95). Mr. Vergara writes that he viewed his mission as documenting in pictures the "discarded and dangerous places" that are rarely traversed by people who do not live or work there. Returning again and again to the same street corner over a decade or more, he provides ample visual evidence of how a neighborhood and even specific buildings deteriorate over the years and disappear. Mr. Vergara's  nine images of 178th Street and Vyse Avenue in the South Bronx, the first taken  in June 1980, show an expansive brick apartment building in various states of decay. By January 1986, all that remains is a crumbling brick facade. In the final photograph, taken in October 1994, four or five new town houses have sprouted up, and two automobiles are parked out front on the street. "Two Bronxes are visible in these photographs: one that died too soon and one too flimsy to last," he writes. There are some signs of hope in his photo gallery: his camera has captured the new homes that have supplanted barren buildings, the tenacious presence of the church in even the most rundown communities and the arresting and colorful murals, many dedicated to black history and tradition, which belie the crime and grime that pervade Mr. Vergara's world. title: The Silent City
author: Erez Yakin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Between the world wars, wordless picture novels were produced by visionary artists like Lynd Ward and Frans Masereel, both of whom were masters of the art  of turning iconic images into acerbic narratives about human folly. After a period of decline, wordless novels have recently enjoyed a small revival as an offshoot of so-called graphic novels, which are themselves offshoots of comic books. Since the wordless novel relies so strongly on visual shorthand, it is often a difficult genre in which to express complex ideas and emotions. THE SILENT CITY (Kitchen Sink Press, paper, $24.95), Erez Yakin's story of the plight of individuals in an industrial totalitarian state, is by no means graphically simplistic; in fact, as Yevgeny Yevtushenko writes in his introduction, "Erez Yakin screams with the silence of his drawings." It is indeed remarkable that such powerfully and exquisitely rendered pictures -- reminiscent of George Grosz and Otto Dix's post-World War I antiwar prints -- were made in 1988, when the artist was just 18 years old. But it is no surprise  that each image is more effective individually than as an element of a complete  story. Mr. Yakin finds it difficult to keep his theme of totalitarian oppression from being a shrill echo of George Orwell's "Nineteen Eighty-four," replete with the common visual clichs of fascist brutality. Nevertheless, "The Silent City" is remarkable for its horrific portrayals of unbridled, demonic power, as well as for the difficult, oppressive darkness of its pictures, which makes them at times barely reproducible. "The Silent City" may not have pushed the limits of the wordless novel beyond what was accomplished in the 1930's, but it proves that Erez Yakin is a virtuoso image maker, a gifted artist at the beginning of what might well be a brilliant career.   Steven Heller

pull_quote: VTAL DUST Life as a Cosmic Imperative. By Christian de Duve. 362 pp. New York: Basic Books. Paper, $14.    WHEN Charles Darwin wrote the "Origin of Species," he deliberately refused to speculate about the first beginnings of life, claiming he hardly knew enough to  make any lasting contribution, and he held back from discussing what he really thought about the mental world of human beings, the highest point of the evolutionary process. Caution was necessary. Excited talk about spontaneous generation of insects occurring after electricity was run through overripe cheeses, and inflammatory, tub-thumping sermons on the miracle of divine creation, made the first stirrings of life on Earth the most perplexing and fascinating problem of the era. Similarly, to discuss the human mind as if its action were nothing more than the mechanical product of the brain might invite a storm of protest. Darwin therefore kept his evolutionary proposals inside strict self-imposed limits -- and was aghast when the hurricane that gathered raged around the very issues he studiously ignored. It is extraordinary how much more  is now known about these mysterious beginnings and endings, the parts of the evolutionary panorama that Darwin left out. Over the last 30 years or so the whole emphasis of research has shifted toward opening up the world of the minute, the vibrant hidden frontiers of life. Christian de Duve's "Vital Dust,"  published in 1995 and now reissued in a welcome paperback format, provides an astonishingly full account of this new story about life, as lucid and engaging as the "Origin" itself. Here is the entire sweep of what is known about living matter.
headline: Stirrings

title: Infamous
author: Joan Joan Henrietta Collins Collins
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: No, INFAMOUS (Dutton, $23.95) isn't that manuscript -- the one Joan Collins's former Random House editors recently described to a Manhattan jury as uneditable piffle. "Infamous" is a later oeuvre, one that Rosemary Cheetham, a top English  editor, proudly offered the same jury as proof that Miss Collins's writing could indeed be redeemed, albeit with extraordinary editorial effort. Having read "Infamous," I now know that Ms. Cheetham committed esthetic perjury, which carries the cruel and unusual sentence of having to read the unpublished Random  House manuscript. Aloud. "Infamous" (on which Ms. Cheetham testified she spent an enormous amount of work) is moderately coherent, all right, but whatever sense of salacious fun Miss Collins may have brought to the manuscript has been  lost. The writing just isn't cheesy enough. With metronome-like dutifulness, "Infamous" tracks the endless travails of Katherine Bennet, an actress popular for her role as a wealthy villainess on a nighttime television soap opera and an obvious stand-in for Miss Collins, who played Alexis Carrington Colby on "Dynasty." If Katherine Bennet is the poisonous Georgia Skeffington on the small screen, everywhere else she is a long-suffering victim -- generous, loving, faithful nad constantly betrayed. But who wants to read a "Gone With the Wind" as told by Melanie Hamilton? By the last 100 pages, it is clear that Ms. Cheetham's insistence that Miss Collins's work can be made readable is just flat-out wrong. The final episodes, in which Katherine realizes that her fabulous new husband is a full- blown psychopath, are so execrably written that  they threaten to give popcorn fiction a bad name. Even the obligatory sex scenes are undercooked.   JAN HOFFMAN

pull_quote: Alicia Ezpeleta has written that rare rabbit book for adults that does not feature the words "with brown gravy" anywhere. Instead, she has produced a delightful compendium of lagomorph lore, profusely illustrated with reproductions of artworks and artifacts culled from a vast array of world cultures -- from ancient Egyptian hieroglyphics to 20th-century American cartoon characters. "Rabbits have represented almost every emotion, ideal, foible and personality trait known to humanity," she writes in RABBITS EVERYWHERE (Abrams,  $24.95), and she goes on to explore the rabbit's role as a symbol for such things as sexuality, fertility, purity, luck and cunning in various societies. The text not only touches on the best known of the literary long-ears -- the Easter Bunny, Peter Rabbit, the March Hare, Br'er Rabbit -- but delves into the  lives of the less publicized as well, including the heroic hares of both Buddhist and African fables. Despite the rabbit's affectionate place in the hearts of many, Ms. Ezpeleta, an interior designer, reveals that a few cultures  weren't very fond of them: the Vikings lumped them in the same category as sea monsters, and the ancient Celts assumed that rabbits purposely lived underground because of their affiliation with darker powers. The giant demon-bunny absconding with a young maiden carved into a portal of the Chartres Cathedral is a little unsettling compared with the familiar images of Bugs and Thumper, and the author even manages to link similar medieval notions of evil to the role of  killer rabbit in the movie "Monty Python and the Holy Grail." Ms. Ezpeleta takes a grand hop through rabbit history, noting along the way that the same creatures used to represent immortality and rebirth in the old Chinese, Greek and Roman legends can be seen even today fulfilling the same role in television's Energizer Bunny commercials.   J. D. BIERSDORFER

pull_quote: Best known of all the Pre-Raphaelite painters, Dante Gabriel Rossetti (1828-82) was the London-born son of a political refugee and the sister of Byron's doctor, as well as the brother of the poet Christina Rossetti. In DANTE  GABRIEL ROSSETTI (Abrams, $29.95), Russell Ash, the author of numerous books on  art, including volumes on Edward Burne-Jones and Toulouse-Lautrec, portrays Rossetti as an undisciplined youth whose florid personal style eventually took him to the center of the Victorian artistic world. Along with his fellow painters William Holman Hunt, John Everett Millais and others, Rossetti founded  the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, a movement Mr. Ash characterizes as having an "idealized and escapist view of an imaginary 'golden age' rooted in the medieval world, with its traditions of courtly love and chivalric duty." Others in Rossetti's circle included the art critic John Ruskin, Burne-Jones, William Morris and the poets Algernon Charles Swinburne and George Meredith. Rossetti, who was also a poet, married his model Elizabeth Siddal in 1855; in 1862 she died from an overdose of laudanum. Racked with guilt that he had ignored her for his work, Rossetti buried the only complete set of his poems with her, and then  ordererd her body exhumed seven years later so that the poems could be retrieved and published. WE live, Julian Barnes suggests in an earlier book, in "a pragmatic and knowing century"; we are also, he says in another, "modern and ignorant." Can we really be all these things? Of course. Knowingness is not knowledge, and pragmatism and modernity are two of our favorite boasts about ourselves. But who is making this diagnosis? In the first case it is Geoffrey Braithwaite, the grieving, widowed doctor and ardent Flaubert fan who tells the story of "Flaubert's Parrot"; in the second, it is the deviser of the brilliant exploration of Gricault's "Raft of the Medusa" in "A History of the World in 10  Chapters." These characters are not exempt from the condition they describe, they are symptoms of it: wry, witty, belated, supposedly practical, often helpless. Behind them hovers the shadowy figure of Julian Barnes himself, who is just as wry, witty and belated, maybe as practical, and presumably quite a bit less helpless. I'm not so sure, though. Style and intelligence, which Mr. Barnes has in abundance, can focus helplessness and allow us to think about something else, but they can scarcely make it go away. Would we want it to go away, in all cases? "How do we seize the past? How do we seize the foreign past? We read, we  learn, we ask, we remember, we are humble; and then a casual detail shifts everything." This is Braithwaite, and "the foreign past," for him, as for Barnes and for us, is delicately weighted with a double meaning: the past of a foreign  scene or a foreign writer, and the past of our own life or marriage or love, which, as L. P. Hartley famously said, is a foreign country. Braithwaite's answer is more than modest, but his initial metaphor is surely too greedy, full  of the promise of failure. We don't seize the past. At best we get a picture of  it, and a couple of chances to revise the picture. And the past, in Mr. Barnes's fiction, becomes a figure for a whole series of separations and gaps, places where the mind or the memory can't quite reach the other side, as if the ferry were becalmed, or the tunnel not complete: between then and now, of course, but  also between there and here, between them and us, between her and him, between any event and the chance of our understanding it.

pull_quote: Mori Ogai's novel THE WILD GOOSE (Center for Japanese Studies, University of  Michigan, cloth, $28.95; paper, $14.95) is a small book that gives immense pleasure. Eloquently understated, it provides a lyrical account of the thwarted  romance between a Tokyo medical student and a young woman who is the mistress of a dull middle-aged moneylender. Written early in this century and translated here with an insightful introduction by Burton Watson, the narrative illuminates the rigid social order of Japan in the 1880's, an era when that country's rapid Westernization was just beginning. Okada, the story's protagonist, is noted for his good looks and virtue. Yet despite his heroic nature, he can't rescue Otama from her fate. The relationship of Okada and Otama consists of furtive glances, a smile, the tip of a hat -- and Okada's rescue of  a pet bird from a snake. The novel's disarming power grows from its minimal plot, its muted descriptions of the two main characters and its narrative viewpoint (the action is seen in flashback through the eyes of one of Okada's schoolmates, a technique that provides esthetic distance). Spare, symbolic imagery reinforces our understanding of all the characters, particularly the women, whose only available responses to disappointment are silent suffering and dissembling. Mr. Watson's introduction outlines the autobiographical elements in the story, and a careful reader may discern Ogai's intimations that he is writing a new kind of fiction. Certainly he was influenced by his substantial reading of European writers, and he ranks as one of the key innovators of modern Japanese literature -- but the success of "The Wild Goose" rests on its timeless portrayal of the clash between social caste and romantic love. Is she crazy? the diners ask one another with a mix of fascination and horror. Doesn't she know about sharks? The swimmer's name is Adele, and by some standards she must be crazy: not so long ago, she turned her back on a pampered, privileged life in the Connecticut countryside to fly off to India and worship at the feet of a tyrannical guru. Seen from the narrator's detached perspective, Adele's headlong pursuit of enlightenment proceeds inexorably, like a 10-car pileup viewed in slow motion far in the distance. As she steadily recedes from her earthly existence, Adele sacrifices not only her autonomy and her material possessions but also a chorus  of bewildered family and friends. She loses weight, her hair becomes streaked with gray, she suffers from mysterious illnesses. But could she be exchanging these mundane measures of health for a deeper spiritual well-being? Is Adele's flight from her former life transcendent or tragic? As it explores these questions, Lily Tuck's second novel emerges as a haunting, strangely perplexing  meditation on the quest for higher meaning -- and the steep price that seekers (not to mention those around them) must pay. title: Frank Stella: An Illustrated Biography
author: Frank Frank Philip Stella Stella
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Frank Stella first caught the attention of the New York art world in 1958, at the age of 22, when his austere "black paintings" marked him as an uncompromising, inventive artist. At 34, Mr. Stella had his first retrospective  at the Museum of Modern Art. Both talented and well connected, Mr. Stella got himself included in the canon of American abstraction with precocious speed. Although his later works -- huge, multipart metallic constructions replete with gaudily colored French curves and graffitilike brushstrokes -- are now most visible as fixtures of corporate lobby art, Mr. Stella has secured a legacy as a masterly interpreter of space, someone who pushed the boundaries of painting. This kind of achievement merits more than the treatment it receives in FRANK STELLA: An Illustrated Biography (Rizzoli, $75). Sidney Guberman, an artist and  Mr. Stella's classmate at Princeton, is diligent about quoting from the best of  what has been previously written about his subject, neither cowed by nor dismissive of what has gone before. But from a close friend -- and well past the halfway mark of Mr. Stella's career -- we expect something extra. Mr. Guberman has plenty of anecdotes from the time he has spent with Mr. Stella over the years, but most of them are not very illuminating. He is at his best when he addresses the art directly, as in his explanations of the relatively complicated working techniques that Mr. Stella used to make his irregular frames and surfaces of serious sculptural depth.   Ted Loos

title: Women In Their Beds: New And Selected Stories
author: Gina Berriault
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: As an alternative to those trivial compendiums of literary opening passages sold near bookstore cash registers, how about a collection of last lines from Gina Berriault's very short stories, WOMEN IN THEIR BEDS: New and Selected Stories (Counterpoint, P.O. Box 65793, Washington, D.C. 20035, $25)? Consider this stand-alone triumph: "He lay facedown under the tree and bit off some grass near the roots, chewing to distract his smile, but it would not give in, and so he lay there the entire day, smiling into the earth." Or: "She heard his breath take over for him and, in that secretive way the sleeper knows nothing about, carry on his life." Ms. Berriault is nothing if not consistent. In these  35 stories, one struggles to find a sentence that is anything less than jewel-box perfect. And the author uses her gift for language to do more than show us the world through her characters' eyes; we are also forced to think about it from their point of view -- no small feat for someone who favors third-person narration. These are complex characters, and although many stories  run only a few pages Ms. Berriault never falls back on cliches: an aging male librarian, for example, is no shrinking violet; instead, he sports "a Borsalino  fedora" and "English boots John Major would covet." Most of Ms. Berriault's characters are caught at moments of divergence: in "Soul and Money," a lapsed Communist confronts God and Mammon in Las Vegas; in "Lives of the Saints," the son of a famous religious artist undertakes his own sort of pilgrimage, visiting his father's works, and discovers that life is more lasting than art. Yet in the smooth flow of Ms. Berriault's writing, few of these people manage to register the emotional pitch needed to transcend their crises. It is not a matter of stoicism; instead, most seem dizzyingly unaware of the option to act on their own behalf. Thus the stories, so exquisite to wend through, leave one a little cold. Like their characters, they seem trapped by the perfection of Ms. Berriault's prose.   Tobin Harshaw

author: Judy William George Wegman Olausen
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: What William Wegman has done for his dogs, Judy Olausen, a photographer who lives in Minneapolis, has done for her mother. But while Mr. Wegman's subjects,  being Weimaraners, look mostly soulful, doleful or moderately embarrassed, Vivian Olausen, a housewife now in her 70's, can personify any affect you can name. And what a game gal she is! In MOTHER (Penguin Studio, $24.95), she allows herself to be dressed up in frumpy housedresses and ratty furs, bedraggled hats and hideous wigs, and, in more than 50 deliriously funny pictures, submitted to any number of indignities. There is a program here: many of the images are a commentary on the lot of women in the 1950's, a period when, Ms. Olausen believes, depressed housewives dragged themselves to the cocktail cabinet or medicine chest for relief (see "Mother's Little Helpers," with Mother spaced out on Valium). Mrs. Olausen, on the other hand, remembers the decade as  one in which she had fun pottering around the house and entertaining, and everyone drank (see "Mother as Enabler"). But while the pictures of Mother carrying a huge wooden cross through the supermarket or chained to an ironing board or, best of all, in pink baby-doll pajamas and marabou mules (pace Marabel Morgan) make a feminist point, others transcend dogma to attain an almost Monty  Pythonesque lunacy. Only consider "Mommy Deer," in which Mrs. Olausen, antlered  and befurred, is tied to the roof of a car. Worth noting, too, that the car is a Plymouth Volare, one of a vast number of authentic, and frequently covetable, props and artifacts that repay careful study. (Remember Ike buttons? Cookie jars in the shape of French poodles? Paint-by-numbers sets?) Pass this book around among your friends, and watch them have conniptions.   Sarah Ferrell

pull_quote: Where are you from?" is a question too often asked of the young, American-born Filipino women who populate M. Evelina Galang's stirring debut collection of stories, HER WILD AMERICAN SELF (Coffee House Press, paper, $12.95). Whether the person asking is a bystander at a bus stop, a school classmate wrinkling her nose at the smell of a box lunch of rice and fish, or a  film director known for his sleazy attitude toward Asian women, none are satisfied when the answer turns out to be Michigan, Wisconsin or New York. But if the ignorance and insensitivity of strangers is borne with graceful yet sarcastic humor, the pressures of home -- under the zealous gaze of parents eager for their daughters to partake of the "land of opportunity" -- yield a frustrated, rebellious sadness. In "Miss Teenage Sampaguita," a visiting aunt observes her brother's tyrannical hold on her niece, who is expected to become a doctor and is deprived of everyday pleasures like the right to date or even talk on the telephone. And in "Talk to Me, Milagros," a silent child watches as her lawyer father, recently arrived from the Philippines, is reduced to working as a busboy in a diner. While a number of Ms. Galang's stories lack a certain dynamic force, all are told in an elegant, mesmerizing style. The finest, "Filming Sausage," is sharp with tension, while the brief, chantlike monologues that frame the collection are as lyrical as prayers.   Abby Frucht

title: Bodies Of Water
author: Rosanne Cash
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Rosanne Cash was born with a microphone in her hand. The daughter of Johnny Cash, she released her first album in 1979 and was immediately recognized as one of country music's freshest singer-songwriters. Those familiar with her much-publicized private life (her marriage to the country star Rodney Crowell, which ended in divorce four years ago, was tabloid manna) will spot bits and pieces of it scattered throughout her first collection of stories and sketches, BODIES OF WATER (Hyperion, $19.95), some of which reads more like autobiography than fiction. But there is no angry score-settling in this pensive book, which takes as its subject the landmarks of a woman's life: love, marriage, childbirth, disillusion, renewal. Unusually for a lyricist, Ms. Cash has a straightforward, sharp-eyed prose style ("I was 22 years old, and my feet  were a little too big for my body. . . . I had two cats -- a serious mistake --  as I had been looking for an image and thought they might help") and, despite a  few awkwardly self-conscious patches, her first book reads like the work of a far more experienced writer. This is not "celebrity" fiction: it is a collection of stories that happens to have been written by a celebrity, and it is very good.   Terry Teachout

title: Catherwood
author: Marly Youman
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Once a barefoot beggar child, the heroine of the poet Marly Youmans's second  novel, CATHERWOOD (Farrar, Straus & Giroux, $20), is brought to live with a noble family in the years after the English Civil War. Something between an indentured servant and an adopted daughter, Catherwood is eventually married off to Gabriel Lyte, who takes her across the Atlantic to a world "fresh and curious" that appears to be "just league after league of woods and swamp and wild river." Feeling herself "the newest of all created things," the young woman confronts her new home, outside Albany, with a keen eye for the "lovely-fierce"  sensuousness of nature. Then one day she and her infant daughter become lost in  the wilderness, and for months they wander about, trying to find their way. Through her harrowing ordeal, Catherwood learns to divest herself of sentiment and fear, including the fear of "man judgment," until she comes to understand that there are "many roads through wilderness, many paths to the city." In describing this process, Ms. Youmans's language is trenchant, graceful and, in places, sumptuously archaic, filled with a richness that provides more than just period color. Her prodigious powers of description render with acuity both small moments and large: the sea crossing, childbirth, snowfall, the slitting of a fawn's throat, the "rammish" stench of a trapper. Ms. Youmans has written a subtle, intelligent novel about one of the most enduring issues in the American  experiment: how to embrace "the world and God" as "better" than men dream.   Philip Gambone

title: From Peep Show To Palace
author: David Robinson
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Compared to today's special-effects-laden blockbusters, early cinematic efforts seem like a yawn. But their eerie realism was so startling to audiences  a century ago that their viewing often incited panic. In FROM PEEP SHOW TO PALACE: The Birth of American Film (Columbia University, $29.50), David Robinson, a film historian, provides a diligent overview from the moment cinema  was just a flicker in a magic lantern to the golden years between 1893 and 1913, when scientists and technicians laboriously fitted together the "pieces in a puzzle" and created feature films. Mr. Robinson's chronology is painstakingly  thorough, if at times tedious, and he dissects the various stages of motion picture development with scholarly zeal. His portrayals of the great cinematic innovators Thomas Edison, the Lumiere brothers and Georges Melies provide some vivid accounts of publicity mongering, patent wrangling and ego interference as  the race for notoriety accelerated. But, finally, the book seems to need a slightly more humorous approach to a subject brimming with pratfalls, and leaves the casual reader craving more anecdotes about the personalities that catapulted the entertainment into the pre-eminent American art form.   Kathryn Shattuck

pull_quote: At the age of 21, Bill Hanna decided that he "would be blissfully happy if I  could make cartoons for the rest of my life." As he says in A CAST OF FRIENDS (Taylor, $22.95), written with Tom Ito, a freelance journalist, Mr. Hanna and Joe Barbera knew they were a winning combination from their first meeting, in 1937. In short order, their collaboration produced Tom and Jerry, the classic cat-and-mouse team. When they founded Hanna-Barbera Productions in 1957, the two were pioneers gambling that their new limited animation techniques would enable cartoons to move from movie screen to television. Huckleberry Hound, Yogi Bear and Boo Boo, the Flintstones and the Jetsons, among many others, were the result. Now 85, still happily at work in his "cartoon quarry," Mr. Hanna pays tribute to wife, family, animation colleagues and employees while giving his two children and seven grandchildren credit for helping him bridge the generation gap. To this day, he watches pencil sketches evolve into exuberant cinematic fantasy and always finds the result "somewhat astonishing." He takes the reader  backstage and lets him feel that excitement. "Cartoons," he says, "symbolize enchantment." The fellow who obligingly screeched and yowled on cue to give voice to Tom and Jerry in the early years has never lost sight of the grand vision that captivated him as a youngster. title: Tumbling
author: Diane Mckinney-Whetstone
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Even the air is palpable in TUMBLING (Morrow, $24), Diane McKinney-Whetstone's engaging first novel about a 1950's community threatened with gentrification. In the working-class black Philadelphia neighborhood that serves as the book's setting, the woeful plaint of Mahalia Jackson records mingles with the perfume of backyard honeysuckle. But the city's insidious attempts to buy out homeowners eventually spill into the domestic world of Herbie and Noon, a young couple whose lives have already been rerouted after not one but two little girls are abandoned on their doorstep. Herbie and Noon are more successful as parents than as spouses and they salve their marital wounds independently: Herbie in a nightclub singer's bed and Noon in her church and in  her fight against the city's plans. But they are true partners in the love and care of their children, especially Fannie, who came first and who charms and frightens them with her occasional clairvoyance. Though the book's end is bluntly forecast from early on and more than a few events are puzzlingly unexplained, the story moves forward on the power of Ms. McKinney-Whetstone's characters. Herbie and Noon's neighbors -- from the meanspirited petty bureaucrat across the street, desperate to protect her meager authority, to the  well-intentioned but miscalculating local pastor, who falls prey to his own pride -- are never merely props. Through these and other deftly portrayed individuals, whose wrongdoing stems more from fallibility than intent, Ms. McKinney-Whetstone captures the formidable struggle to protect both a community  and a family.   Lise Funderburg

THE British novelist, playwright and journalist Angela Huth's lovely new book, "Land Girls," is a war story about the real heroes of World War II: not the generals but the ordinary citizens who left their workaday lives and fought  for their country as best they could. The girls of the title were young women who joined Britain's Land Army; they left the safe, tea-cozy world of traditional female jobs -- university student, hairdresser, sweetheart -- and went off to take up the exhausting, dawn-to-darkness labor of agricultural work  so the male farm workers could take up arms. At first blush, there is nothing exceptional about the three main characters. When gentle, cerebral Agatha, romantic Stella and fluff-brained Prue first assemble for their tour of duty on  the Lawrence farm in Dorset, the reader might be deceived into thinking this is  going to be yet another banal three-girls-meet-somewhere-and-become-friends novel, the sort in which there is inevitably one suicide, one ghastly abortion,  a slew of beastly men and a great display of passive aggression. But the reader  would be wrong; there is not one moment of melodrama in the entire book. And there is absolutely nothing banal about these women.

title: Cezanne: Landscape Into Art
author: Francoise Cachin
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: No painter has been so hallowed by his fellow artists as Paul Cezanne. Picasso called him "the father of us all," Klee "the supreme master," Matisse "a kind of benevolent god of painting." Yet despite a century's influence and an abundance of literature that has successively denounced, extolled and interpreted his work, Cezanne remains an enigmatic artist, his impact on subsequent generations more quantifiable than his artistic intentions. In the introduction to CEZANNE (Philadelphia Museum of Art/Abrams, $75), an exceptionally handsome catalogue raisonne produced in conjunction with a traveling exhibition currently at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, Francoise Cachin, director of the Musees de France, and Joseph J. Rishel, a curator of European painting at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, make no claims to providing new interpretations of either the artist or the man. Instead they concentrate on the shifts of Cezanne's critical fortunes. The result is a fascinating patchwork of opinions that illustrates not only how Cezanne has been reinvented as the patron saint of each successive movement from Fauvism to Cubism to early abstraction, but how monumentally important he remains. Each reproduction is accompanied by a short text that provides the provenance of the work, bits of biography, excerpts from letters and occasional anecdotes, as well as details about Cezanne's technique. More academic and less accessible is Pavel Machotka's CEZANNE: Landscape Into Art (Yale University, $45). Mr. Machotka, who teaches psychology and art at the University of California, Santa Cruz, has photographed the sites of Cezanne's landscape paintings, with an eye to approximating the spot and precise time of day that Cezanne painted each scene. He then attempts to analyze Cezanne's way of working, noting the correspondences as well as the changes between place and painting. The result is fascinating to look at, though frequently pedantic.   Andrea Barnet

THE German occupation of France and its factious fallout provide the raw material of Brian Moore's powerful new novel. Between 1940 and 1944, more than one in four of the 330,000 Jews living on French territory were deported. The majority were identified, arrested and shipped off by French administrators and  the French police, without whose zealous cooperation German forces in France would have been unable to carry out the job. In a time of want, fear and national humiliation, few of the French cared about what happened to the Jews. While many individuals helped them (otherwise three in four would not have survived), many also denounced, pursued and robbed them. The drumbeat of official Vichy propaganda presented Jews as noxious parasites, and the church went along, fearing godless Communists more than godless Nazis. Some bishops --  and, in their wake, some priests -- denounced such injustice, but most Roman Catholics had other priorities. Objectively, the church, like its Vichy allies,  shared in the vicious anti-Semitic policies of those dark years.

title: The Photographs Of Dorothea Lange
author: Keith F Davis
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: Dorothea Lange (1895-1965) was a complex woman who excelled at making straightforward images. To show things as they are was the challenge she set herself; to her that meant a simple and direct portrayal of people firmly rooted in their time and place. Lange moved from New York to California in 1918, having picked up her technical training by doing odd jobs in Manhattan studios. She became friends with a circle that included Imogen Cunningham and Ansel Adams, and for a time ran a successful portrait business. During the early years of the Depression, when breadlines and picket lines formed in San Francisco, she began  to photograph trouble in the streets. Subsequent work in the 1930's focused on rural poverty and migration, which she documented for studies directed by her husband, the economist Paul Taylor, as well as for the Farm Security Administration. THE PHOTOGRAPHS OF DOROTHEA LANGE (Hallmark Cards/Abrams, $35) includes her famous images, like "Migrant Mother," as well as those from other,  less well-known series, like those on the internment of Japanese-Americans in 1942, on war workers in a California shipyard and on a California public defender's office. By her choice of perspective, use of gesture and framing, Lange's photographs convey her empathy and passionate belief in human dignity. The book, with text by Keith F. Davis, who has written extensively on American photography, reflects Lange's taste with its spare presentation of 85 reproductions and accompanying quotations or comments, a device Lange often used herself.   Rosemary Ranck

pull_quote: In a hefty and companionable volume, entitled simply COLLECTED STORIES (Sun and Moon, $24.95), Djuna Barnes's biographer Phillip Herring has gathered 43 of  her stories, written from 1914 to 1942. Perhaps best known for her 1936 novel, "Nightwood," Barnes displays in her shorter work an unflagging taste for the grotesque: In "The Head of Babylon," a Polish-American farmer marries off his quadriplegic daughter, who sits on a great dais between two candles and suddenly declaims a strange, biblical speech as she leaves with the groom. In "No-Man's-Mare," a captured wild horse, bearing a dead woman to the undertaker,  veers from a path and disappears into the sea. Although Barnes experiments with  narrative, her stories generally depend on a plot ending with an O. Henry twist, a format suited no doubt to the newspapers and magazines for which she often wrote. Her characters are not round, nor do they sustain and engage us with their conflicts. Rather, they are haunting emblems of human weakness, vice and,  occasionally, virtue. Most striking is Barnes's particular use of language, which aligns her with Pound, Joyce and Stein: syntactical inversions, epigrams,  puns, cliches and one-liners crowd her sentences. Witty and passionate, her stories are often reflexive, with asides to the reader and a sardonic tone that  mocks the characters. And always they reflect Barnes's bleak view of existence. pull_quote: The Nazi era was captured largely in black-and-white photographs. The primary visual records of Hitler, Nazi Party rallies, book burnings, ghetto roundups, even the Nuremberg trials, are colorless. Leni Riefenstahl used black and white  to glorify her subjects in "Triumph of the Will." Fifty years later Steven Spielberg shot "Schindler's List" in monochrome to echo the collective memory. But in 1939 an amateur film club shot color movies of the theatrical parades and pageants leading to the opening of the House of German Art, which Hitler built as a monument to Volk culture. This extraordinarily well-preserved, candid record of Nazi pomp, circumstance and banality was released a few years back by  the BBC as a documentary with the title "Good Morning, Mr. Hitler!" WEEKEND IN MUNICH: Art, Propaganda and Terror in the Third Reich (Pavilion/Trafalgar Square, $40), by Robert S. Wistrich, a professor of modern European history at the Hebrew University in Jerusalem, is a selection of stills from this amateur film, sandwiched between a history of Nazi propaganda that was not part of the BBC program and comments by spectators at the festival. The book is disquieting  in the way these color photographs do, in fact, reduce Nazi villains to everyday people. Color somehow defangs even the most heinous of the bunch, like Heinrich  Himmler and Julius Streicher. Yet the most disturbing image of all is not in color; it is a black-and-white snapshot of two pageant participants drinking Coke in front of a German Coca-Cola sign.   Steven Heller

Chance encounters lead to quick romance, and even a rambunctious yet doomed marriage, though the ghost of his first love weighs heavy. True to his word, this most quick-witted of comedians nimbly sidesteps his fractious childhood as Irwin Kniberg -- a "very angry, very tough kid" who was thrown out  of every high school in Brooklyn -- to get to the good parts, which began when he was 15 and landed his first job as a comic in the Catskills. Mr. King tells priceless stories about Bugsy Siegel (his patron during the Las Vegas days, "when everybody I worked for got killed"), Frank Sinatra (who was declared the winner of their tomato sauce cookoff by judges named Willie the Nose and Morey the Mouth), and a host of other beloved old cronies including Jack Benny, Joe E. Lewis, Milton Berle and Sammy Davis Jr. But like the cocky street fighter he once was, Mr. King has an instinct for someone's weak spots, so the stories that really floor you are about wounded comrades like Dean Martin and Judy Garland. As for his own underbelly, Mr. King allows as how he's got a rotten temper and carries around a load of rage. (But he has nothing but compassion for his father, a Jewish immigrant embittered by real poverty and imagined failure.) "Most comedians are angry, it's their edge," he says. "When I get angry, I'm better." Mr. King leaves it to his wife, in a sweet and unaffected chapter called "Jeanette's Turn," to bring up uncomfortable subjects like the comedian's jaw cancer and certain unspecified problems with their children. We always knew  that Alan King was a funny guy; now we know what made him so keen and caustic.   Marilyn Stasio

author: Mary Kay Zuravleff
outlet: The New York Times Book Review
pull_quote: At the outset of Mary Kay Zuravleff's engaging first novel, THE FREQUENCY OF  SOULS (Farrar, Straus & Giroux, $23), we learn a crucial piece of information about its hero, an electrical engineer named George Mahoney. It seems that from  the time he built his first radio set "from glass tubes and a spool of lead," George has been convinced that "the universe was soldered together with logic."  So it isn't surprising that he reacts with "fatherly embarrassment" to his new junior office mate's revelation that she experiments with radio frequencies in order to listen for the dead. In fact, George knows that Niagara Spense, who is  partly deaf in one ear, has difficulty hearing many things. What is surprising -- most of all to George himself -- is that, despite his disbelief, Niagara inspires in him "a burning curiosity that had not flared in some 20 years." And  in no time curiosity becomes obsession. When he awakens his wife, Judy, yelling, "Niagara," she replies, "You had better be screaming about vacation." For George, who has had no complaints or extramarital liaisons during his largely unexamined 16-year marriage, Niagara is an improbable love object. Ungainly, untidy and chaotic, she is the antithesis of Judy, "a Georgia brand of Southern  belle." But Niagara's presence makes George aware of the fine line between contentment and stagnation. As he explains it, "If you leave a car parked long enough, the tires go flat and the battery won't hold a charge." By the end of the novel, when Niagara and her research have enabled George to recapture a few  sparks, Ms. Zuravleff's insightful yet gentle rendering of the absurd has also allowed readers to connect fully with her quirky and endearing characters.   Janet Kaye
